It is not among his collected sayings, the earliest trace these notes could find is a 2016 management blog already calling it ‘often attributed’, and ‘continuous improvement’ is the business-school name for kaizen, which only became common English in the 1980s, seventy-odd years after Twain died.
cards.why: Put the fake one next to the hospital corridor. On the same night, two people hand two others the same advice about not waiting for perfect, and both sign it with a borrowed name: Jamie's Voltron, Michelle's Twain. The advice is good both times. And keep the real one in your pocket. ‘When in doubt, tell the truth’ is not a bad line to hand a man with a son who is going to ask him hard questions.
cards.source: Mark Twain, Following the Equator (1897), ‘Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar’ chapter epigraphs; Mark Graban, Lean Blog (2016) on the ‘often attributed’ line; Masaaki Imai, Kaizen (1986). Michelle's lines per the episode's transcripts.
cards.groundingNotes: Both of Michelle's Twain lines are in the Forever Dreaming transcript, and lassoism has the second; the A.V. Club, Seat42F and Fangirlish confirm the Twain book and her habit of quoting him. ‘When in doubt, tell the truth’ is documented in Following the Equator (University of Virginia Twain library; twainquotes.com; WIST). ‘Continuous improvement is better than delayed perfection’ is absent from Wikiquote's Twain page; Lean Blog (2016) calls it often attributed; the kaizen link is via Wikipedia. Absence of evidence is stated as such, not as proof. The card no longer stakes anything on whether the book is about London or Europe: ‘time abroad’ is Michelle's own phrase.

cards.title: Two divorced people talk properly, and stay divorced
cards.moment: Over a long pub evening, Ted and Michelle talk honestly about the divorce and about the years since. She names his isolation, tells him to start seeing someone, and has a specific person in mind. Neither of them is angling to undo anything.
cards.idea: Almost every story about a former couple reaching real understanding treats the understanding as a stage on the way back to each other — as if getting each other right and getting back together were the same movement. This scene separates them. They arrive at a genuinely accurate account of what happened and of who the other person is now, and that account points away from reconciliation rather than towards it. The note she leaves reportedly says the same thing in one line: the divorce is not the failure.
cards.why: For a show whose central claim is that people are worth the effort of understanding, this is the harder version of the claim — understanding someone properly does not entitle you to keep them. It is also the episode quietly upgrading Michelle from backstory to person: she has her own work, her own reasoning about her own life, and opinions about Ted that she is not obliged to act on.
cards.source: Episode reviews at But Why Tho, Show Snob, Seat42F and The Cinemaholic.
cards.groundingNotes: Four reviews agree on the substance and on the pointed absence of reconciliation. They differ on the note’s exact wording and on how much Michelle says about her own relationships, so the card does not fix either.

cards.tag: Explained to a room you were not in
cards.title: The kindness and the betrayal are the same act
cards.moment: Gemma tells Alice the squad does not dislike her — they simply do not know her. It lands, and it is true. Then Lizzie mentions in passing that Gemma had already taken Alice’s worries to the team.
cards.idea: Nothing happened twice here. One event is both the advocacy and the injury, and there is no version of the advocacy that does not contain the injury: to speak for someone you have to hand over the part of them they had not chosen to hand over. Alice’s specific privacy was the fact that she was struggling. Gemma spent it on her behalf, kindly, and got her a warmer room in exchange for the one thing she was keeping.
cards.why: It is much sharper ethics than the romantic misunderstandings running alongside it in this episode, and it is the same question the show asked about Ted in season one, when Trent Crimm decided what to print. Being understood is not free. Somebody has to do the explaining, and the explaining is a disclosure, whoever is doing it and however well they mean it.
cards.source: Episode recaps at Show Snob, Ready Steady Cut and Comic Basics.
cards.groundingNotes: Three independent recaps agree on both halves of the beat: the reassurance, then Lizzie revealing where it came from.

cards.title: The vanity is still there. It just is not driving
cards.moment: Jamie is back, blond again, launching a vodka called Apple Tartt: dancers, a themed entrance, the whole apparatus. The bottle artwork distorts his face, and he knows it. Later he walks out of his own launch party to sit in a hospital with Roy.
cards.idea: The detail worth watching is the bottle. He explains it himself later that night: the first label was perfect, he kept wanting it better than perfect, and that is how it ended up wrecked. The Jamie of season one would have blamed the designer. This one tells the story against himself, and then turns it into advice for somebody else.
cards.why: This is what growth looks like when a show declines to sand a character down: he did not become humble, he became someone whose self-regard no longer outranks other people. The test is the exit. He leaves the party that is entirely about him, on the night it happens, for the man who used to be his enemy.
cards.source: Episode coverage at MovieWeb, The A.V. Club and Comic Basics.
cards.groundingNotes: Three sources confirm the brand, the launch, the distorted bottle art and Jamie leaving to take Roy to hospital. Season review 2026-10-12: CORRECTED: he does mind the bottle; he tells Rebecca the label was ruined by his wanting more than perfect (Forever Dreaming transcript, lassoism).

cards.title: Two songs, fifty years apart, jammed into one sentence
cards.moment: The title card, read against the scene it is named for: Roy on a dance floor for roughly one chorus before his knee ends the evening.
cards.idea: It is a collision of two songs that want opposite things. Duke Ellington recorded the tune in May 1940 as an instrumental called ‘Never No Lament’; Bob Russell put a lyric on it in 1942 and it became ‘Don’t Get Around Much Anymore’ — a standard sung by a man who has stopped going out. House of Pain’s ‘Jump Around’ (1992, produced by DJ Muggs of Cypress Hill) is the other thing entirely: the record stadiums put on to get an entire stand off its seats, still doing that job at Camp Randall decades later.
cards.why: The title puts the going-out song and the staying-in song in the same breath, which is exactly the shape of the episode. Everyone is out; Ted stays in and gets the better night. Roy jumps around and is punished for it immediately. And the joke has an ache under it — the standard is about a man who could go out and no longer wants to, while Roy is a man who wants to and no longer can.
cards.source: Duke Ellington, ‘Never No Lament’ (1940), lyric by Bob Russell (1942); House of Pain, ‘Jump Around’ (1992).
cards.groundingNotes: Both songs verified against their own records. Three recaps confirm ‘Jump Around’ is the song Roy is injured to; the Ellington half of the title is plain from the construction.

cards.tag: The same knee, the same Jamie
cards.title: It went stopping Jamie. Now it goes dancing with him
cards.moment: Jamie talks Roy onto the dance floor at his own vodka launch. About one chorus later the knee goes, and Jamie drops the entire party to take him to hospital and sit with him there.
cards.idea: That knee has a Jamie Tartt attached to it. Episode 4 gave you its history: the Season 1 finale, Roy running Jamie down to stop him scoring against Manchester City, and the injury that ended his playing career. Now the same joint has failed twice in front of the same man: once chasing him, once dancing beside him.
cards.why: You could not draw the arc more plainly if you tried, and the show does not comment on it, which is why it works. The first time, the knee cost him a career and he was doing it against a boy he could not stand. This time it costs him a party, and the boy carries him out.
cards.source: Ted Lasso S1E10, The Hope That Kills You, and S2E1, Goodbye Earl; episode recaps.
cards.groundingNotes: Season-one injury and season-two retirement confirmed against the episode record. Three recaps confirm the recurrence and that Jamie takes him to hospital.

cards.tag: Attributed to, and then attributed again
cards.title: Jamie’s philosopher is called Voltron
cards.moment: In a hospital corridor, with Roy's knee being seen to down the hall, Rebecca admits she wrecked something by needing it to be perfect. Jamie recognises the problem from his vodka label, and offers her a maxim: perfect is the opposite of good. He credits it to Voltron. Rebecca suggests he means Voltaire. Jamie wonders why she has brought a cartoon robot into it.
cards.idea: The maxim is real, and it is the one filed under Voltaire: le mieux est l’ennemi du bien, the best is the enemy of the good. But Voltaire did not claim it either. In Questions sur l’Encyclopédie (1770) he offers it as an Italian proverb, il meglio è l’inimico del bene, and in his 1772 verse tale La Bégueule he hands it to an unnamed wise Italian. Montesquieu had written something very close in his Pensées decades before that. The line everyone credits to Voltaire is a line Voltaire went out of his way to credit to someone else.
cards.why: So Rebecca's correction is right, and also not the end of it: Voltaire was quoting too. This is the season's running joke about wisdom. The line Ted quoted at the dartboard was credited to a Whitman who never wrote it; the half-time line last week gets credited by everybody to a Nin who never wrote it; and before tonight is out, Michelle will hand Ted a Twain who never said hers. A saying survives by being repeated, and being repeated is exactly what wears the author's name off it. Rebecca takes the advice. It works.
cards.source: Voltaire, Questions sur l’Encyclopédie (1770) and La Bégueule (1772), with the Montesquieu antecedent in his Pensées.
cards.groundingNotes: Two recaps independently report the Voltron misattribution. The wording of Jamie’s line is reviewers’ paraphrase — no transcript was reachable — so the card paraphrases rather than quotes. The provenance of the maxim is documented. Season review 2026-10-12: Sharpened from the transcript: Rebecca corrects him on screen, and Jamie takes Voltaire for the robot. The maxim is set up by his own vodka-label story. The blossom line is no longer counted as the show's misattribution (see s4e5-blossom-quote-attribution). Season review 2026-10-12: Corrected: there is no sign over the dartboard; in S1E8 Ted says he saw the line painted on a wall.

cards.tag: The punishment ends when it ends
cards.title: See you at work
cards.moment: At midnight the team turns up outside the Crown & Anchor with Alice among them, suspended since the last episode. Michelle sends Ted out. He wishes Alice a happy new year and tells her he will see her at work, as if nothing had happened.
cards.idea: There is a real position buried in that shrug. A sanction is meant to be a fixed quantity — it runs, it ends, and the person walks out of it owing nothing further. What usually happens instead is that the formal punishment ends and an informal one continues indefinitely: the wariness, the shortened leash, the thing everyone remembers. Ted refuses the second half, and refuses it in public, in one sentence, in front of the team who watched her get suspended.
cards.why: This is the same instinct that made Roy forgive Nate quickly, and the show has been argued with about it before — whether letting someone off that fast treats them as a full moral agent or as someone who cannot be held to much. Here it reads as the generous version, because Alice had to cross a room to be there at all. The suspension did its work. Extending it would only have done work on her.
cards.source: Episode reviews at DMTalkies and The Film Gordon.
cards.groundingNotes: Two reviews report the reinstatement in compatible terms; no third source and no transcript was reachable, so the card keeps to the substance of the exchange rather than its wording. Season review 2026-10-12: Now four sources; the line is ‘at work’, not ‘at practice’, and Michelle sends him out (transcript, lassoism, Cinemaholic).

cards.title: The man who hands out belief gets handed some
cards.moment: After midnight Ted comes back in to find a freshly painted BELIEVE sign waiting for him. Michelle made it, on what was left of Henry's school-project paper, and propped a short note beside it.
cards.idea: Psychologists have a name for the specific failure this scene fixes. Igor Grossmann and Ethan Kross called it Solomon’s paradox — after the king renowned for the counsel he gave everyone else and the disaster he made of his own household. Across three studies with 693 participants, they found people reasoned markedly less wisely about their own close-relationship problems than about the identical problem handed to them as a friend’s. The remedy that worked was not more thinking. It was self-distancing: describing your own situation in the third person, as though it belonged to somebody else. The gap closed.
cards.why: Ted's whole method is one sentence on a sheet of paper, and the one person he cannot hold it up for is himself. That is not hypocrisy and it is not a plot hole; it is the ordinary shape of the thing, and it is why the sentence has to arrive from outside, in someone else's hand. And this episode tells you whose hand it always was. Earlier that night Ted remembered Fort Scott, his first head-coaching job, where Michelle kept writing him little notes and making signs for his office wall. The BELIEVE sign has an origin story, and it is her.
cards.source: Igor Grossmann and Ethan Kross, ‘Exploring Solomon’s Paradox’, Psychological Science 25(8), 2014, pp. 1571–1580.
cards.groundingNotes: Five independent recaps agree on the scene and the sign; they differ on the note’s exact wording, so the card paraphrases. Solomon’s paradox is a pairing offered for the idea, not a reference the show is making. Season review 2026-10-12: Michelle made it on Henry's school paper (Seat42F, Cinemaholic). The Fort Scott memory is in the Forever Dreaming transcript and lassoism; Fangirlish reads these scenes as giving the sign an origin story.

cards.tag: The song was a poem first
cards.title: What is playing under the opening montage
cards.moment: Before the title card: childcare falling through, a rent rise, a car that will not start, a delivery shift squeezed in around training, an internship interview that clashes with practice. It runs under TLC’s ‘Unpretty’ — 1999, from FanMail.
cards.idea: The song did not start as a song. Tionne ‘T-Boz’ Watkins wrote it as a poem from a hospital bed, after watching a talk show in which men held forth on how women look; Dallas Austin later built the record around it. Watkins was diagnosed with sickle-cell anaemia as a child and has been in and out of hospital since she was seven. The subject is the distance between what a person is actually worth and the valuation the world keeps reading back to her.
cards.why: That is the episode’s argument, moved off bodies and onto pay slips. The montage is not scene-setting; it is the thesis, stated in the only place the show can state it without anybody making a speech. Whoever chose the track chose a song written by a woman insisting on her own value while her body was failing her, and laid it over women insisting on theirs.
cards.source: TLC, ‘Unpretty’ (LaFace/Arista, 1999), written by Tionne Watkins and Dallas Austin, from FanMail.
cards.groundingNotes: Two independent reviews name the track over the cold open. The poem origin, the songwriting credits and Watkins’s sickle-cell anaemia are confirmed on Wikipedia; her 1999 collection Thoughts is not sourced as the poem’s home, so that claim is left out.

cards.tag: Naming it instead of fighting it
cards.title: A break-up conducted as an act of accuracy
cards.moment: Erin ends it herself. Her reason is not a grievance; it is an observation. Roy is still in love with Keeley, something he let slip while heavily medicated over New Year. She does not argue the point, bargain over it, or ask him to try harder. She says what is true, declines to carry on under those terms, and tells him he is worthy of the person he loves. He does not deny any of it.
cards.idea: Most television break-ups are a contest over whose account of the relationship wins. This one is a piece of clear seeing offered as a gift. She has less standing in the scene than he does — she is the newer attachment, the one with more to lose by naming it — and she is nonetheless the one insisting on the truth. That is not weakness dressed as grace. It is a refusal to spend months on something she can already see the shape of.
cards.why: Watch how much of the kindness is in the framing. She does not tell him what he is doing wrong; she tells him what he deserves. The same fact, delivered as an accusation, would have made him defensive and made her small. Delivered as a release, it leaves them both intact. It is a useful thing to have watched before you ever need it.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 7, ‘Yes & Baby’; the break-up and its stated reason are reported across eight independent recaps.
cards.groundingNotes: Eight independent recaps agree on who ends it, why, and how gently; two trace her certainty to his medicated admission at New Year.

cards.title: Beard buys a new face
cards.moment: Somebody called him old over the New Year. He turns up to work in a new shirt and blue contact lenses, one of which promptly pops out. It fools precisely nobody, least of all him.
cards.idea: This is the episode’s opening song acted out by a man. ‘Unpretty’ is about reaching for the purchasable fix instead of the wound underneath, and Beard has gone and bought the fix — a surface answer to a question asked at depth. The show puts the argument in the women’s changing room as a matter of money, and then quietly repeats it in the men’s as a matter of vanity.
cards.why: Notice that nobody laughs him out of the building. Beard is the show’s most self-contained character, and here he is doing the least dignified thing a person can do about ageing. Watch what he changes: not the habits, not the situation — the eyes. The one part of him people actually look at.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 7, ‘Yes & Baby’; reported across six independent recaps. The pairing with ‘Unpretty’ is a reading, not a stated intention.
cards.groundingNotes: The tan, the blue contacts and the ‘old’ remark around New Year are reported by six independent recaps. The connection to the opening song is offered as interpretation only. Season review 2026-10-12: Tan and brown eyes are not in any source opened in the season review and are removed; the lens popping out is in the transcript.

cards.tag: A web with words in it
cards.title: The first thing Archie reads off the sign is ‘Some pig’
cards.moment: Lizzie has to bring her four-year-old, Archie, to work. He looks up at the BELIEVE sign and ‘reads’ it as Some pig, because his mum has been reading him Charlotte's Web. Later Beard reads him the end of the book and chokes up.
cards.idea: In E. B. White's 1952 novel, Charlotte is a spider who saves her friend Wilbur, a pig, from slaughter by weaving words into her web above his pen. The first words she writes are Some Pig. People read them, decide Wilbur must be remarkable, and treat him that way. The words on the web do not describe his value so much as make the world notice it.
cards.why: Which is exactly what a sign over a door is for, and exactly the argument this episode has with its own. By the end, the women have added words of their own to BELIEVE, and the person who reads the amended sign out loud, for the first time, is Archie. A sign with a word on it, changing how the world values someone: the show did not have to explain the joke, and it doesn't.
cards.source: E. B. White, Charlotte's Web (1952). Archie's ‘Some pig’ and Beard reading him the ending per the episode's transcript and recaps.
cards.groundingNotes: Season review 2026-10-12: Added from the commentary pass. Archie's ‘Some pig’ reading, the Charlotte's Web connection and Beard reading him the ending are in the Forever Dreaming transcript and reported by But Why Tho, The Cinemaholic and Fangirlish. Archie's age (four) is from the transcript. Book facts from Wikipedia. The reading of the sign as a web is this card's interpretation; the link to the book is on screen.

cards.title: What the squad is actually asking for
cards.moment: Inside the argument about the BELIEVE sign, one point is about money. These players already believe, they say, or they would not be playing second-division football for peanuts.
cards.idea: Kept carefully separate from the fiction, because the show never says which league Richmond’s women play in: English women’s football only introduced minimum salary requirements across its top two tiers very recently, worked out over about eighteen months with the Professional Footballers’ Association. The league has not published the figures — its own chief operating officer says the level differs by age group and by division. That is how young the idea of a guaranteed full-time wage is in this sport.
cards.why: It is the one complaint in the room no sign can answer, and the show lets it stand. The men's side has never once had to have this conversation.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 7, ‘Yes & Baby’; real-world context from Sport Resolutions’ report on WSL and WSL2 minimum salaries agreed with the PFA.
cards.groundingNotes: The confrontation is confirmed by five independent recaps. The real-world comparison is deliberately number-free: the league publishes no salary figures, the candidate’s bands were single-sourced, and the show never names the league Richmond’s women play in. Season review 2026-10-12: CORRECTED: there is no separate scene of the players taking pay to Ted; the remark is part of the sign argument (Forever Dreaming transcript and recaps).

cards.title: The two words the episode is named after
cards.moment: Alice comes back determined to agree with everything, and a training session buckles under the weight of it. Ted and Beard take her aside and hand her the improviser’s upgrade: agreeing is only the first half. The second half is putting something of your own into what you have just accepted — and Beard supplies the flourish that finishes the episode’s title.
cards.idea: ‘Yes, and’ is the most quoted rule in improvised theatre and nobody can say who wrote it. It is not in Viola Spolin’s Improvisation for the Theater; the Spolin estate’s own essay on the phrase describes it as something that came into use after she codified the first method, and argues she would have rejected it in favour of her own principle of following the follower. Wikipedia’s entry names no originator either. It is a genuinely authorless idea — a practice the form grew rather than a doctrine somebody handed down.
cards.why: Watch what the correction actually fixes. Saying yes to everything is not generosity; it is abdication, and Alice’s version of it makes her less present, not more. The ‘and’ is where the person doing the agreeing is required to show up. That is the difference between being accommodating and being a collaborator, and it is the note the whole episode is written on. (After a Whitman who never wrote his line and a Nin who never wrote hers, a rule with no author at all makes a nice change.)
cards.source: Gary Schwartz, ‘The Trouble With “Yes, And…”’, spolin.com (the Viola Spolin estate’s site).
cards.groundingNotes: The scene is confirmed by eight independent recaps. The origin claim is deliberately narrow: no source locates a coiner, and the Spolin estate places the phrase after her work rather than in it. The candidate’s Compass Players / Del Close lineage could not be corroborated and is not asserted here.

cards.title: The sign walks into a room it cannot answer
cards.moment: The BELIEVE sign goes up in the women’s changing room, and for the first time in four seasons the room argues with it. They are not short of belief; team unity is about as high as it has ever been. What is in the way is everything in the opening montage: childcare, rent, a car that will not start, a second job, an interview that clashes with practice.
cards.idea: This is the show auditing its own central idea, and it does not flinch. Optimism is a strategy for problems that are made of attitude. It is not a strategy for problems that are made of money and time. A slogan that has carried the men’s side for years turns out to be addressed to a difficulty these players do not have — which is not a failure of the slogan so much as evidence that it was always speaking to a particular kind of person about a particular kind of obstacle.
cards.why: Ted’s method has been tested before by cynics and by grief. It has never been tested by material circumstance, and the honest answer is that it does not reach. Watch how the episode refuses to make anyone wrong here: the sign is not mocked and the players are not scolded. Something can be true and still be the wrong thing to hand someone.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 7, ‘Yes & Baby’ (Apple TV, 16 September 2026); reading corroborated across six independent reviews.
cards.groundingNotes: Six independent reviews report the same beat and the same reading — the players already believe, and the obstacles named are childcare, rent, transport and second jobs.

cards.title: Two more words, on a Post-it
cards.moment: Alice does not defend the sign and she does not take it down. She adds to it — a Post-it stuck underneath that extends the single word into a second clause about winning. The moment lands when Lizzie’s small son reads the amended sign out loud, which nobody in the room knew he could do.
cards.idea: Look at the shape of what she just did. She accepted what she was handed and then put something of her own into it. That is the improv rule the episode spent the first half teaching her, performed on the show’s own creed rather than on a training drill. The lesson did not stay in the classroom.
cards.why: It also solves the hand-me-down problem. A sign carried over from the men’s side is a loan; a sign the women amended is theirs. And notice who certifies it — not a coach, not a captain, but a child sounding out words for the first time in front of everybody. The show keeps putting its most important sentences in the least official mouths.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 7, ‘Yes & Baby’; the Post-it and the boy reading it are reported across seven independent recaps.
cards.groundingNotes: Seven recaps report the Post-it amendment; four independently report Lizzie’s son Archie reading it aloud. One recap stages his reading differently, so the card describes the beat without fixing the exact staging.

cards.title: Bantr comes back around
cards.moment: Ted, stuck on the very first question, sits down with Keeley to build a profile on her old dating app. It is not the app's only appearance: in the opening montage two of the women players, who have just agreed to a break, are matched with each other by it. Ted eventually deletes his account and goes and asks someone out in person instead.
cards.idea: Bantr was Keeley’s PR side hustle two seasons ago: a dating app with no photographs, where you had to be judged on what you wrote. Its whole premise was that the picture is the least informative thing about a person. Four seasons on, the show hands it to the man who has spent the series insisting on the same thing about footballers, and he cannot make it work.
cards.why: The gag about the matched couple is the app telling the truth its users did not want — they are on a break and the algorithm still says these two. And Ted deleting the profile is not a defeat. He built the thing, read it back, and decided the honest version of the question had to be asked out loud, to a face.
cards.source: Bantr, introduced in Season 2 as Keeley’s photo-free dating app; its return reported across six recaps of this episode.
cards.groundingNotes: Six recaps report Ted’s profile and its deletion; two independently report the two players being matched with each other. The Season 2 origin comes from secondary coverage — the Ted Lasso wiki page would not open.

cards.title: Three words Ted cannot find, and then can
cards.moment: The dating profile asks him to describe himself in three words and he seizes up completely. He can find three words for Keeley in a second; for himself, nothing. What he eventually arrives at is a plain statement that he is someone who can be loved. Then he deletes the profile, walks to the theatre, asks the stage manager out in person — and she says no, because she is already seeing someone.
cards.idea: Look at what the episode refuses to do. Having let him say the thing out loud, it declines to reward him for it. The claim and the outcome are kept in separate compartments on purpose: being lovable is a description of a person, not a prediction about how an evening will go. If the no had made the claim false, the claim was never worth making.
cards.why: This is the same man who could not fill in the first box. The distance between those two moments is the whole arc, and none of it is about her answer. What changed is that he was willing to be told no in person rather than not be asked at all — which is exactly the thing he has been asking of everyone else since the day he arrived.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 7, ‘Yes & Baby’; the self-description and the refusal are reported across six independent recaps. Paraphrased here rather than quoted.
cards.groundingNotes: Four independent recaps report the same three-word self-description (differing only in spelling) and all six agree on the in-person approach and the polite refusal.

cards.title: Dolly Partonberg, agent, of Chicago
cards.moment: An agent who represents both Dani and Roy is bluffing Richmond, inventing rival interest to force the money up. Rebecca's answer is not a lawyer. It is a prank call: Rebecca in an American accent, and Zelda as Dolly Partonberg, a recruitment officer from the Chicago Fire, staying in character long enough to call the bluff. It works, and it earns Zelda a formal advisory job at the club.
cards.idea: In an episode about accepting the offer and adding to it, the person who takes the principle furthest is not on the pitch. Zelda is handed a bluff and, rather than refusing it, she raises it: builds a second fiction on top of the first until the first one collapses. The name is doing most of the work, absurd enough to be obviously fake and delivered with enough conviction that nobody thinks to check.
cards.why: A small object lesson in the difference between lying and performing. Watch the confidence rather than the content — the reason it lands is not that the story is good, it is that she never once steps outside it. And note what Rebecca does with the result: she does not thank her and send her away, she gives her a desk.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 7, ‘Yes & Baby’; the alias and its Chicago provenance are reported by three independent reviews.
cards.groundingNotes: Three independent sources report the Dolly Partonberg alias and the Chicago cover story. Recaps disagree on which player’s agent is being outplayed, so the card leaves the client unnamed; no source supports any link between the fake Chicago agent and the show’s own improv history, so none is claimed. Season review 2026-10-12: CORRECTED: Zelda does not invent a rival agent; she poses as a Chicago Fire recruitment officer, with Rebecca as an American assistant (transcript; But Why Tho). The agent, Derrick Tarp, represents both Dani and Roy, settling the earlier disagreement.

cards.title: These two have worked together before
cards.moment: A production note rather than a scene. Dr. Erin Beaumont is played by Laura Haddock — who has been here with Brett Goldstein before.
cards.idea: They co-starred in SuperBob (2015), the mockumentary Goldstein co-wrote and led as a postman handed superpowers; Haddock plays June, a librarian he is set up to date. Before that they were both in a 2013 short, For Life, which later grew into the AMC series Soulmates.
cards.why: It explains something you can feel in the scenes without being able to name. The ease between them is not entirely acting; these two have shared a screen, on and off, for more than a decade.
cards.source: SuperBob (dir. Jon Drever, 2015); casting background via The Cinemaholic and The A.V. Club’s recap of this episode.
cards.groundingNotes: SuperBob is confirmed from Wikipedia and named in the episode’s A.V. Club recap. The 2013 short For Life rests on The Cinemaholic alone — IMDb would not open — so the card attributes that part rather than asserting it flatly. Season review 2026-10-12: Corrected: June is someone Bob is set up with, not someone he dates. For Life (2013) is now confirmed by Screen Slate and both actors' Wikipedia pages; whether their For Life characters are a couple is unclear, so the ‘third go at almost-romance’ framing is dropped.

cards.title: BELIEVE gets amended by committee
cards.moment: In the opening montage, hands keep reaching up to the taped-together sign above the door. One player adds a note that turns it into a threat; another softens it into a pleasantry. By the end of the sequence it is buried in Post-its.
cards.idea: Two reviews read it as the squad taking last week's improv lesson (accept what you are handed, then add something of your own) and applying it to the oldest object in the building. Which is a genuine change in what the sign is. For three seasons it was Ted's: put up by him, torn down, taped back together, handed on. Here it is edited by the people standing underneath it, without asking. And later in the episode Ted adds a note of his own.
cards.why: A creed you are given is a rule. A creed you are allowed to write on is yours. The show has spent a long time on whether Ted’s belief survives without Ted in the room, and this is the most economical answer it has offered: it survives by being defaced.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 8, ‘Follow the Anger’; the montage is described across three independent reviews.
cards.groundingNotes: Three reviews confirm the Post-it montage and two read it as an extension of the previous episode’s ‘yes, and’ lesson. Sources disagree on whether Ted adds a note himself, and the wording of individual notes is single-sourced, so neither is stated here. Season review 2026-10-12: Resolved: Ted does add a note, ‘and let it out’, at the end of his changing-room speech (Cinemaholic, Seat42F, LadyGeeks and the transcript).

cards.tag: She knows exactly what she cost her
cards.title: The coach who left her on was once the player who came off
cards.moment: Richmond are comfortably ahead and Gemma has already scored twice. The coaches could take her off; Alice leaves her on to chase a hat-trick. Minutes later Gemma's knee goes and she leaves on a stretcher.
cards.idea: Alice Chilton was a footballer before she was a coach, and her career was ended by repeated cruciate ligament injuries. Coaching was how she stayed near the game she had been taken out of. She is therefore the one person in that stadium who knows, in detail and from the inside, what she has just handed her striker.
cards.why: This is why her collapse later is not ordinary professional guilt. Most remorse is imaginative — you picture what the other person is going through. Hers is memory. Watch her in the scenes that follow and you are watching someone being made to live it twice, once as the player and once as the person who caused it.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 8, ‘Follow the Anger’; Alice’s injury history is given in cast interviews with Tanya Reynolds.
cards.groundingNotes: TVLine and the Variety and Hollywood Reporter cast interviews all give the ACL backstory and the Arsenal academy detail. Two independent recaps confirm that Alice kept Gemma on hoping for a hat-trick. Season review 2026-10-12: ‘Arsenal academy’ removed: the season review found it in Looper alone, and Alice's club stays unnamed as in Episode 2. Gemma's age is given nowhere, so ‘nineteen-year-old’ is removed.

cards.tag: The real thing behind the storyline
cards.title: Why a knee injury is the crisis a women’s club dreads most
cards.moment: A knee gives way in a match Richmond are already winning, and the club discovers it has no functioning medical answer.
cards.idea: Episode 2 gave you the headline: women footballers tear this ligament at several times the rate men do (FIFPRO says two to six times, and some football-specific studies put it higher). The less-quoted half is what comes after. A smaller share of players get back to their old level, and re-tears within five years are common. Nobody agrees on why the gap exists. Anatomy, the hormonal cycle, boot and pitch design, training loads, and decades of thinner medical provision for women’s teams are all argued for. One large cross-league study found the rate varying about fourfold between women’s leagues, some with no gap against the men at all, which points hard at conditions rather than bodies.
cards.why: Note what the show does and does not say. Ted talks about an MRI on her ACL and runs through the grades of ligament injury, but nobody gives her a diagnosis; she waits. And it makes the club's failure administrative rather than medical, which is why that variation between leagues matters. If the same injury is far likelier in one league than another, the difference is not anatomy. It is what the club decided to pay for.
cards.source: Sky Sports, Future of Football; British Orthopaedic Association; peer-reviewed reviews of sex-specific injury risk in football.
cards.groundingNotes: Sky Sports, the British Orthopaedic Association and peer-reviewed reviews agree on the elevated rate, the worse return outcomes and the contested causes. The show does not name Gemma’s injury as a cruciate tear, and this card does not either. Season review 2026-10-12: CORRECTED: the show does name the ACL (Ted mentions an MRI on it, per the transcript); it gives no diagnosis.

cards.title: The reason nobody looks at her knee
cards.moment: Rebecca leans on the club doctor to see Gemma quickly, and finds out what Richmond has actually been asking of him. He signed on when the club had one team; now it has two, and he is not going to stretch. When she threatens to fire him, he resigns, and Gemma waits at home, undiagnosed.
cards.idea: The injury is not what breaks the club. The staffing is. Richmond announced a women's side and then quietly assumed the existing medical provision would cover it. A second team is not an addition to a club; it is a second set of everything a club is made of.
cards.why: Notice the order the episode puts things in. A knee gives way, and then nothing happens — no urgency, no diagnosis, no plan. The drama is manufactured entirely out of a line item. It is a sharp piece of writing about how institutions actually fail people: rarely by cruelty, usually by having declined to fund the thing they announced.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 8, ‘Follow the Anger’; reported across three independent recaps.
cards.groundingNotes: Two recaps give the doctor’s pay complaint and three the resulting delay; only one says he leaves the club altogether, and his surname is spelled two ways across sources, so neither detail is stated here. Season review 2026-10-12: CORRECTED: Dr Strudwick quits over workload, not pay (transcript; recaps). Pay is never mentioned. The id is kept for stability.

cards.tag: Last week’s grace, this week’s appointment
cards.title: The woman who let Roy go is the one who takes the call
cards.moment: With the club's own doctor gone, Keeley asks Roy whether Dr Beaumont might see Gemma. By the time the squad reaches the hospital, Erin is Gemma's doctor.
cards.idea: Erin is a doctor; that is how Roy met her, as a patient. She is also the woman who ended things with him one episode ago by calmly naming the truth — that he was still in love with Keeley — and telling him to go and be with the person he loved. The show now has the person she named ring her for a favour, and has her grant it without visible cost.
cards.why: This is the show quietly declining a cheap option. There was an easy version where the ex-girlfriend is frosty and the new couple pay for their happiness, and the episode does not want it. The generosity Erin showed in ending it turns out not to have been a one-off gesture but simply how she is, and the proof arrives a week later in the least romantic form available: a professional favour, done properly, for a player neither of them knows well.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 8, ‘Follow the Anger’, following Episode 7, ‘Yes & Baby’.
cards.groundingNotes: Three independent sources report Keeley’s call and Erin taking on Gemma’s care; the season cast list and IMDb confirm Erin Beaumont is a doctor. Season review 2026-10-12: Keeley's call is off screen: she raises it in the car, and Erin mentions it at the hospital (transcript).

cards.title: Ted does nothing, and it is the most deliberate thing he does all year
cards.moment: He finds Alice in pieces, with the squad still training. He does not offer a fix, and he does not produce one of his stories with a lesson folded inside it. He sits down beside her, and they breathe.
cards.idea: The show has spent four seasons on a man whose instrument is talk. Here it takes the instrument away from him and the scene works better. What Alice needs is not information, a reframe, or absolution; she needs to not be alone in the room while it passes. Ted appears to know the difference, and the knowing is the whole performance.
cards.why: Watch what he does not do. It is the least Lasso-like scene the show has written, and several critics called it the best of the season. If you have ever sat with someone and worried you had nothing useful to say, this is the episode making the case that you were already doing it.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 8, ‘Follow the Anger’; the scene is described in the same terms across four independent reviews.
cards.groundingNotes: Four independent reviews describe the scene identically, two of them noting Ted is handling his own panic attack in the same moment. Season review 2026-10-12: Reviewers' reading of Ted managing his own panic is unsettled (TVLine, quoting Tanya Reynolds, frames it as Alice's panic attack), so it is no longer stated.

cards.title: Someone once did this for him
cards.moment: Ted lowers himself next to a colleague who is crying and simply stays there.
cards.idea: Reviewers read it as a deliberate answer to Season 1, Episode 7 — the Liverpool trip, where Ted has his first full panic attack while Rebecca is singing, stumbles out of the bar, and Rebecca comes out after him and sits with him. That was the first time those two ever spoke to each other without a pretence in the way. It is the hinge the whole friendship turns on.
cards.why: Nobody in the scene mentions it and the show does not cut back to it. It simply gives him the other chair, six years on. Kindness in this programme is rarely invented on the spot; it is usually something a character is passing along because it was once done for them, and here you can point at exactly when.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 8, ‘Follow the Anger’, read against Season 1, Episode 7, ‘Make Rebecca Great Again’.
cards.groundingNotes: Two independent reviews name the Season 1 callback; Wikipedia confirms the S1E7 scene — the karaoke, Ted’s first panic attack, Rebecca following him outside.

cards.tag: The line he turned inside out
cards.title: Ted reverses the most famous sentence in American sports cinema
cards.moment: In the changing room, after finding his assistant coach in pieces, Ted tells the players that football has crying in it, and runs through the greats who have wept to prove it. Nobody there needs to hide what they feel, apologise for it, or carry any shame about it. Then he reaches up and adds two words of his own to the sign.
cards.idea: He is inverting a line most Americans know by heart. ‘There’s no crying in baseball!’ is Tom Hanks, as the washed-up manager Jimmy Dugan, in A League of Their Own (1992) — ranked 54th on the American Film Institute’s list of the hundred greatest movie quotations. The film is about the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League, a real women’s league founded while the men were at war, and it was directed by Penny Marshall, the first woman to direct a film past a hundred million dollars at the box office. In the same speech Ted reaches for Beaches (1988) — directed by Garry Marshall, Penny’s older brother, who also turns up in A League of Their Own as the sweet manufacturer who founds the league.
cards.why: So the sentence Ted flips and the weepie he names came from a brother and a sister. And the film he is arguing with is itself about a women’s team that had to prove it belonged — which is the argument this whole season is having. Jimmy Dugan barks that line at a woman who is crying. Forty-odd years of story later, an American coach stands in front of a women’s side and says the opposite.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 8, ‘Follow the Anger’. A League of Their Own (1992, dir. Penny Marshall); Beaches (1988, dir. Garry Marshall); AFI, 100 Years…100 Movie Quotes (2005).
cards.groundingNotes: The Hollywood Reporter recap names the baseball line as what Ted is flipping, so the reference is reported rather than inferred. Every film fact — director, cast, AFI rank, the league, the Marshall siblings — is confirmed on Wikipedia.

cards.title: Messi is the first witness, not the only one
cards.moment: Making the case that crying is not a failure of nerve, Ted starts with Messi, a man he says shows less emotion than the Mona Lisa, and reminds the room of the state he was in when he finally won a World Cup. Then he keeps going: Ronaldo, Maradona, Zidane, Neymar, and Roy Kent at his own retirement.
cards.idea: It is a well-chosen lead witness. Messi wept openly after Argentina won the 2022 final, and those pictures went round the world. He wept again on 19 July 2026, after Argentina lost the final to Spain in extra time. And a strange footnote: at the half-time show of that same 2026 final, Jason Sudeikis and Brendan Hunt appeared in character as Ted and Beard to introduce Justin Bieber.
cards.why: The argument only works because of who it starts with. Ted could have named a sentimental player and been waved away. Instead he opens with the one whose composure is proverbial, which turns the point from a plea into an observation: this already happens, at the highest level there is, and nobody thinks less of him for it.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 8, ‘Follow the Anger’; Messi’s tears at the 2022 and 2026 World Cup finals are widely reported.
cards.groundingNotes: The Hollywood Reporter recap and a transcript excerpt both have Ted naming Messi and the World Cup he won. Al Jazeera covers the 2022 tears, ESPN and the ABC the 2026 ones. Season review 2026-10-12: CORRECTED: Messi is not Ted's only example (transcript; Rolling Stone Brasil). The 2026 final (Spain 1–0 Argentina after extra time, 19 July) and Messi's tears are confirmed by Khaleej Times and AP via the Chicago Sun-Times; the half-time appearance by Billboard, CP24 and La Capital. The sign's spelling varies by outlet and is not stated.

cards.tag: Bob Dylan, 1967, sung by the theme tune
cards.title: What is playing on the Underground
cards.moment: Roy and Keeley, stuck on a crowded Tube carriage after the car fails him, passengers getting on and off around them while neither of them moves. The track over it is ‘When I Get My Hands on You’ by The New Basement Tapes.
cards.idea: That record has an unusual history. In 1967, in the months after his motorcycle crash, Bob Dylan wrote a box of lyrics he never set to music. Decades later his publisher handed them to the producer T Bone Burnett, who put five musicians — Elvis Costello, Rhiannon Giddens, Taylor Goldsmith, Jim James and Marcus Mumford — in a room at Capitol Studios for two weeks to write music for words that had been waiting forty-seven years. The 2014 album is the result. This track is Mumford’s: he shares the music credit and sings the lead.
cards.why: And Marcus Mumford wrote and performs the Ted Lasso theme, with Tom Howe. So in the scene where Roy finally stops waiting, the voice on the soundtrack is the show’s own — singing words that sat in a box for half a century before anyone gave them a tune. Whether or not that was the intention, it is a good joke on a man who has taken four seasons to say something out loud.
cards.source: The New Basement Tapes, ‘When I Get My Hands on You’, from Lost on the River (2014), lyrics by Bob Dylan, produced by T Bone Burnett; ‘Ted Lasso Theme’ by Marcus Mumford and Tom Howe.
cards.groundingNotes: A season soundtrack listing and a review both place the track in this episode, and the listing pins the artist, ruling out the unrelated 1973 single of the same name. The album’s origin, Mumford’s lead vocal and co-writing credit, and his authorship of the show’s theme are all independently confirmed.

cards.title: Roy takes the honour and talks about someone else
cards.moment: He did not want to go. The car defeated him, the Underground nearly did, a scooter finished the job, and by the time he reaches Stamford Bridge most of the ceremony has dispersed. He speaks anyway, to a handful of people, and the speech turns out not to be about football.
cards.idea: One reviewer reads the whole day as a man who cannot accept praise rather than one who is indifferent to it — which are easy to confuse from the outside and entirely different underneath. Indifference would have simply not turned up. Roy spends a whole episode failing to arrive at a thing he is unable to sit still for, and the fact that he keeps travelling is the tell.
cards.why: Watch what he does with the microphone when he finally has it. Handed a formal occasion for being told what he is worth, he uses it to tell someone else what she is worth, and ends by telling Keeley he is worthy of her: Erin's own parting words from last week, handed on. That is how this character has always done sincerity: never straight at the target, always at a slight angle, and always about somebody else first.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 8, ‘Follow the Anger’; the sequence is reported across five independent recaps.
cards.groundingNotes: Five independent recaps agree on the resisted ceremony, the failed journey, the near-empty room and the speech turning into a declaration to Keeley. Season review 2026-10-12: ‘Worthy of you’ echoing Erin's words in Episode 7 is in both episodes' transcripts.

cards.tag: A real wall, and who got there first
cards.title: Roy’s tribute is on a piece of terrace that actually exists
cards.moment: Roy finally arrives at Stamford Bridge for his place on Chelsea's Shed Wall, to a room that has largely emptied out.
cards.idea: The wall is not invented for the show. It is built from the surviving stretch of the old Shed End terrace at Stamford Bridge, and it carries portraits, statistics and biographies of Chelsea legends — Peter Osgood, Ray Wilkins, Peter Bonetti, Frank Lampard, John Terry among them — with QR codes so visitors can read their way along it. In 2024 Emma Hayes was added, on her departure after twelve years and fifteen trophies in charge of Chelsea Women. She was the first of the women’s legends to appear there.
cards.why: Which is the quiet joke of putting this scene in this episode. The show sends its fictional Chelsea legend to collect his place on a wall that, in life, only recently made room for a woman, in the week its story is entirely about whether a women's team gets a doctor. And there is history on that wall: Ray Wilkins is on it, and in Season 3 the show digitally altered a real Chelsea banner remembering Wilkins to read ‘Roy’, and had to apologise for it. Roy has now joined him properly.
cards.source: Chelsea FC on the Shed End tribute to Emma Hayes (2024); Other Media, who built the Shed Wall installation.
cards.groundingNotes: Chelsea’s official site confirms the wall, the legends named on it, and Hayes as the first Chelsea Women legend added, in 2024. The studio that built it confirms the old-terrace construction and the QR codes. Season review 2026-10-12: Ray Wilkins banner per Wikipedia's page for S3E2 (‘(I Don't Want to Go to) Chelsea’), which records the apology, and two further reports; Wilkins on the real wall per Chelsea FC.

cards.tag: Attributed to Watergate, not from it
cards.title: The title is a correction to a line nobody actually said
cards.moment: Higgins has found supporters quietly selling their shares in the club, some of them for far more than the shares are worth, and cannot work out who is buying. Mae makes a show of throwing him out of the pub, then, out of sight round the side, tells him to follow the anger.
cards.idea: It is a deliberate swerve away from the instruction everybody reaches for, which is to follow the money. And here is the thing about that one: it is not a piece of Watergate history. It is a line written for the 1976 film All the President’s Men by the screenwriter William Goldman, spoken by Hal Holbrook as Deep Throat. It does not appear in Woodward and Bernstein’s book, and Mark Felt, who was revealed as Deep Throat in 2005, is not documented saying it. Fifty years of journalists and prosecutors have quoted as investigative doctrine a sentence a screenwriter made up.
cards.why: Keep count, because the season has been. A Whitman who never wrote the line Ted quoted at darts; a half-time line in Episode 5 that the world credits to an Anaïs Nin who never wrote it; Jamie’s Voltron and Michelle’s Twain on the same night in Episode 6. This time nobody repeats the famous misquote: Mae steps straight past it. And her version does real work in the plot. Money tells you who benefits; anger tells you who has a grievance, and a grievance will make someone pay well over the odds for a thing that cannot repay them. Mae is pointing at motive rather than profit, which happens to be the better question here.
cards.source: All the President’s Men (1976, dir. Alan J. Pakula, screenplay by William Goldman); NPR, ‘Follow The Money: On The Trail Of Watergate Lore’ (2012).
cards.groundingNotes: Four recaps confirm Mae’s line and the share-buying. NPR traced ‘follow the money’ and found it absent from the book and undocumented from Mark Felt — it is Goldman’s screenplay. Setting the two lines against each other is this app’s reading, not a stated intention of the show. Season review 2026-10-12: Corrected: Mae says it outside, after pretending to throw Higgins out, not in the pub (transcript and recaps). Her reasoning, that a buyer after money would act openly, supports the motive-over-profit reading. Season review 2026-10-12: Corrected: there is no sign over the dartboard; in S1E8 Ted says he saw the line painted on a wall.

cards.title: The crying episode was written by the writers of Ted's worst hours
cards.moment: The credits: written by Jamie Lee and Brett Goldstein, directed by Erica Dunton.
cards.idea: Jamie Lee also wrote ‘Man City’, the eighth episode of Season 2, in which Ted finally tells the club psychologist what happened to his father. Brett Goldstein wrote ‘The Signal’, two episodes earlier, in which Ted's panic attack takes him off the touchline mid-match. Between them, these two put the show's lead's hardest season on screen.
cards.why: So the writers who put Ted's worst hours on screen have now written the one where he sits with somebody else through theirs and tells a room full of professionals that crying at work is allowed. The same people built the wound and, five years of television later, the answer to it. Goldstein also co-wrote the episode in which his own character is honoured on a legends wall and then declines to talk about himself.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 8, ‘Follow the Anger’, written by Jamie Lee and Brett Goldstein; Season 2, Episode 8, ‘Man City’, written by Jamie Lee.
cards.groundingNotes: Two independent reviews give this episode’s writer and director credits; Wikipedia confirms Jamie Lee as the writer of ‘Man City’ and what happens in it. Season review 2026-10-12: CORRECTED: the touchline panic attack is in S2E6 ‘The Signal’, written by Goldstein; ‘Man City’ (Jamie Lee) is the confession to Dr Sharon (Wikipedia for both episodes).

cards.title: One life starts in the same hour another ends
cards.moment: Keeley faints in the stands at the women’s match, works out why, confirms it with more than one test, sits on it for most of the episode, and tells Roy once the promotion is won.
cards.idea: Structurally the hour is a pair of brackets with a trophy in the middle: a pregnancy at one end, Mae’s death at the other, promotion in between. Nothing in the dialogue connects them. The episode simply schedules them on the same afternoon and lets you do the arithmetic: the club’s next generation announces itself on the day it loses the woman who had pulled its pints for all of the last one.
cards.why: This is the oldest trick in storytelling and it is a trick for a reason: a birth read next to a death is not two pieces of news, it is one idea about time. Worth noticing how little the episode leans on it. No cross-cut, no music cue tying them, no one saying anything about circles. Two things happen on the same day, which is what days are like.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 9, ‘Mae Rides the Bus’; the beats are confirmed across five independent recaps.
cards.groundingNotes: Five recaps confirm the faint, the realisation, the tests, keeping it from Roy and telling him at the end. How far along she is differs between accounts — six weeks, eight weeks, about two months — so no figure is given, and the report that she tells Rebecca first over lunch could not be confirmed and is left out.

cards.tag: Last week’s decision, made the other way
cards.title: The episode restages the mistake and lets them both get it right
cards.moment: Gemma is cleared after her scan, plays, wins a penalty and scores it — and the knee starts talking to her again. At half-time Alice says she is done. Gemma does not argue.
cards.idea: Episode 8 was the same decision with the opposite answer. Richmond were comfortably ahead, Gemma had two goals and wanted the third, Alice let her stay on, and the knee went. Here the game is not won, the player has a reason to stay out there, and the coach takes her off anyway, and the player who fought to stay on last week accepts it.
cards.why: This is the cleanest piece of construction in the episode and it is done without a single line of explanation. Neither of them refers back to it. You are simply shown the same fork in the road a week later and allowed to notice that two people have changed. Watch Alice’s face when Gemma does not fight her; it is the only apology either of them gets.
cards.source: Season 4, Episodes 8 and 9; reported across five independent recaps.
cards.groundingNotes: Four recaps confirm the medical clearance, five the penalty, five that she does not play the second half, and three that Alice makes the call and Gemma accepts it. One account describing her as uncleared refers to an earlier scene, before the clearance. Sources differ on whether the knee flares in the first half or later, so no minute is given. Season review 2026-10-12: ‘Nineteen-year-old’ removed: no source gives Gemma's age.

cards.tag: Not sexism in general. A resolution, with a date
cards.title: The thing Mae was shut out of was shut by a committee
cards.moment: In the away dressing room before the deciding match, Mae tells the Richmond women what she wanted as a girl and could not have: she says, in passing, that women were not allowed to play officially.
cards.idea: You met this ban in Episode 5, behind Keeley’s empty seats: on 5 December 1921 the Football Association declared the game ‘quite unsuitable for females’ and shut women’s matches out of its members’ grounds until 1971. What that card left out is how thoroughly it was enforced. Almost every usable pitch in England belonged to an affiliated club, so in practice it was a ban. When teams tried cricket and rugby grounds instead, the FA leaned on those bodies too, and registered referees lost the work.
cards.why: Watch the line again knowing that. She is not saying nobody encouraged her, or that the boys would not pick her. She is saying the governing body of the sport wrote her out of it in a minute of a meeting, and kept her out for her entire girlhood. The episode never says the word ‘FA’, which is why the line can sound like a general complaint about the old days. It is not. It is a specific administrative act, and it has a date.
cards.source: The Football Association’s resolution of 5 December 1921; histories of the ban and of its lifting in 1971. The episode itself does not name the FA or the year.
cards.groundingNotes: The 1921 resolution, its wording, its reach and the 1971 lifting are confirmed by four independent sources. The speech is confirmed by six recaps and two write-ups that quote it; she says women were not allowed to play officially, and does not name the FA or any year, so this card does not claim she does. One recap places the speech at half-time rather than before kick-off, and one paraphrases it as being about talent rather than permission; both are outliers.

cards.title: Her whole girlhood fits inside the ban
cards.moment: Mae’s speech, read against the dates.
cards.idea: The show has never told us how old Mae is, so this has to be done carefully. Annette Badland was born in August 1950 and was 76 when the episode went out, and Mae is written as a woman of that generation. For an Englishwoman born around 1950, the FA’s recognition of the women’s game in 1971 arrives at about twenty-one. Every year in which she might have been coached, picked, given a kit or given a pitch falls inside the fifty years the game was closed. Not most of them. All of them.
cards.why: Listen to both halves of what she says: that women were not allowed to play officially, and then, getting a laugh, that she was not much good anyway. The joke is real, and also beside the point. Nobody gets to find out whether they would have been good at something they were never allowed to try. Worth saying plainly: the arithmetic here is the card's, built on the actress's age. The episode does not give Mae a birthday.
cards.source: Annette Badland, born 26 August 1950; the FA ban, December 1921 to 1971. Mae’s age is never stated in the series.
cards.groundingNotes: Badland’s birth date and age are confirmed by two independent sources, and the ban dates by two more. The character’s age is not established anywhere — the show has never given it — so the sum is an inference from the actress’s generation and is flagged as one in the card. Season review 2026-10-12: CORRECTED: Mae does also say she was not very good (transcript; E! confirms ‘officially’), which contradicted the card's old line about what a woman who was never any good would say.

cards.tag: She had the choice and she took the cheap seats
cards.title: Offered the owner’s box, she goes and stands with the fans
cards.moment: At Bristol, Mae is offered a place in Rebecca’s box. She goes into the supporters’ end instead, and someone else takes the seat upstairs.
cards.idea: The whole day is people giving Mae things she was never given: a seat on the team bus, the dressing room, the floor to speak. The box is the last and grandest of them, and it is the one she declines. Which is the only one of them that would have taken her out of the crowd. She has spent four seasons behind a bar watching other people watch football; what she wanted was not to be waited on, it was to be in the noise.
cards.why: Note what this does to the ending. She dies in the stand, among supporters, having chosen to be there over an upholstered seat with the owner. The episode could have had her collapse in a private room with Rebecca beside her and made it a scene about Rebecca; it put her in the crowd instead, and made it a scene about Mae. And watch her in that stand when the music goes up. The song is ‘Jump Around’, the one from Episode 6's title, and Mae is dancing.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 9, ‘Mae Rides the Bus’; reported in four independent recaps and a cast interview.
cards.groundingNotes: Four recaps and a cast interview agree she turns down the box for the supporters’ section. One write-up instead describes her beside Rebecca at the moment she collapses; the two are not flatly incompatible, but the disagreement is real and this card claims only the choice, not where she was in the final seconds. Season review 2026-10-12: ‘Jump Around’ as Mae dances in the stand is reported by four sources; it is not connected here to her collapse.

cards.tag: A small thing in an episode full of them
cards.title: The keeper who had never worn gloves puts gloves on
cards.moment: Boots has been keeping goal bare-handed because she prefers it. In this match she breaks a finger. At half-time Beard talks her into the gloves, and the second half goes differently.
cards.idea: It plays as a throwaway and it is the episode’s theme in miniature. The gloves are not a technique she lacks; they are help she has been refusing on the grounds that she does not need it. The broken finger does not change her ability, it changes what refusing costs the team. So she takes the equipment, and the save that turns the game comes after she does.
cards.why: Put it next to the other two: Mae accepts a lift she would not ask for, Gemma accepts a substitution she would once have fought. Three people in one afternoon accept something they had been declining, and all three are better off. The show does not line them up for you, which is exactly why it is worth lining them up yourself.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 9, ‘Mae Rides the Bus’; reported in four independent recaps.
cards.groundingNotes: Four recaps confirm the broken finger, the gloveless habit, Beard persuading her and the change mattering to the result. One recap calls the goalkeeper by a different name; four call her Boots.

cards.tag: Six years of setup, one goal
cards.title: The girl with the ball scores the one that seals it
cards.moment: Richmond go two goals down at Bristol and come back to win 4–2. Shannon scores, and three recaps have her goal as the one that clinches promotion.
cards.idea: Shannon is the girl from the park Ted kept running into in Season 1. They have a proper kickabout in the second episode, and she turns up again and again, including in the queue at Trent Crimm's book signing in Season 3's final montage. In Episode 3 of this season Ted signed her over both his coaches' doubts. Here she scores the goal that takes Richmond up.
cards.why: The show has never made a speech about her. She was a recurring joke about how football-mad this corner of London is, and she has been sitting in the background for six years with a ball under her arm. Then the club builds a women's side and the joke turns out to have been a plan.
cards.source: Ted Lasso S1E2, Biscuits, and her recurring Season 1–3 appearances; Season 4 Episode 9 recaps.
cards.groundingNotes: Six recaps confirm Shannon scores in the 4–2 win and three that her goal seals promotion; nothing calls it her debut, so that is not claimed here. The kickabout is placed in Episode 2 on the authority of that episode’s own director, who says she is not in the pilot, plus a contemporaneous recap; one feature says the pilot and is contradicted. Recaps disagree about the other goalscorers, so they are not listed. Season review 2026-10-12: ‘Trent Crimm's book about Ted’ corrected: in the Season 3 finale Ted has the book retitled precisely because it is not about him.

cards.tag: Everything important happens just out of reach
cards.title: The show refuses to let you watch the worst minute
cards.moment: As the match ends, Mae is already on the ground when we reach her. A steward interrupts Rebecca to say there has been an incident. Rebecca takes Ted aside, and their conversation plays out under a song rather than in words you can hear.
cards.idea: Count what is withheld. You do not see her fall. You do not hear what the steward says beyond the fact of it. You do not hear Rebecca tell Ted, and you are never told on screen that Mae has died at all — that arrived afterwards, from the cast in interviews. Everything the hour is actually about is placed one remove away: behind glass, under music, off the edge of the frame.
cards.why: This is a choice about what the camera is for. A show that wanted you to cry would have held on her face. This one hands you the shape of the news and lets you do the rest, which is roughly how the news arrives in life — secondhand, from someone with a job to do, in a room where everyone else is still celebrating. The restraint is the technique, and it is why the scene keeps working on a rewatch when you already know.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 9, ‘Mae Rides the Bus’; the staging is described the same way across five independent recaps, with the death confirmed in cast interviews.
cards.groundingNotes: Five independent sources give the same sequence: Mae found collapsed, a steward’s report of an incident, an inaudible exchange between Rebecca and Ted scored to a song, and no on-screen statement that she has died. The death itself was confirmed by cast members after broadcast, not by the episode. Season review 2026-10-12: ‘After the final whistle’ softened: whether the collapse comes during or after it is unclear across sources.

cards.title: The season turns on a throwaway shareholding
cards.moment: Late on, Zelda's associate Hugo finally sits down with the Milk sisters about their shares. Rebecca and Higgins are still looking at Rupert. By now, you are not.
cards.idea: The Milk sisters are the elderly minority shareholders, 2.9% of Richmond: the stake Rupert got hold of years ago in his fiancée's name, on his way to trying to take the club back. Rebecca sold 49% of the club to its supporters at the end of Season 3, and this episode spells out what that cost her: she keeps control only for as long as the sisters keep hold of theirs. The whole thing is a rounding error with a doorbell.
cards.why: What makes this satisfying is that the show is not inventing leverage; it is cashing a cheque it wrote years ago in a scene that was played as a joke about two tiresome old women. Watch the ownership thread with that in mind. The 49% Rebecca gave away for the right reasons is also the 49% that now has to be fought for.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 9, ‘Mae Rides the Bus’; the earlier buyout from the Season 1 episode record; Rebecca’s 49% sale from the Season 3 finale.
cards.groundingNotes: The 2.9% figure, the earlier buyout in the fiancée’s name, Rebecca’s 51% after selling 49% to the fans, and Zelda working through Hugo are each confirmed by two or more sources. Accounts disagree about which season the sisters were first mentioned, so no season is given here. Season review 2026-10-12: CORRECTED: removed the claim that Rebecca holds 51% and a buyer can reach 49% and no further; the finale's 49/49 arithmetic cannot be reconciled with it, and no source states her holding going in. Rebecca and Higgins do not rule out Rupert in this episode; they still suspect him at the start of Episode 10. The control line is in the transcript.

cards.tag: An old question about when a life can be judged
cards.title: She is given the thing, and then the hour ends
cards.moment: The gap between Mae’s speech, the promotion being sealed, and her collapse in the stand is a matter of minutes.
cards.idea: There is a very old idea under that shape, and it is worth having in mind even though the show never points at it. In Herodotus, Solon refuses to call the richest king alive happy; he will call him fortunate, and reserve the other word until he hears the man has ended his life well, because luck can still undo everything. Aristotle takes the puzzle seriously rather than dismissing it — in the first book of the Nicomachean Ethics he asks whether we must see the end, and says that one day, or a short time, does not make a man blessed. Happiness, on that view, is a property of a whole finished life, not of a very good afternoon.
cards.why: Solon’s worry is that a good life can be spoiled at the last minute. The episode arranges the opposite and makes you feel it: the last minutes are the ones that complete the thing. Annette Badland has said in interviews that Mae was having one of the best days ever and went in the best way she could have — which is the same judgment Solon says you can only make once it is over. To be clear, this is a frame brought to the scene, not a reference the episode makes.
cards.source: Herodotus, Histories I.30–32 (Solon and Croesus); Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.10. Annette Badland in post-episode interviews.
cards.groundingNotes: Both passages were checked at the text: Herodotus I.30–32 and Nicomachean Ethics I.10. Badland’s comments are confirmed in two interviews — she says Mae was having one of the best days ever and went in the best way, which is paraphrased rather than stretched here. The episode makes no reference to either philosopher; the frame is the card’s.

cards.tag: The last card on screen is for someone else
cards.title: The episode ends by remembering Rupert’s actor
cards.moment: After Rebecca tells Ted what has happened, the picture goes black and a card comes up: in memory of Anthony Head.
cards.idea: Head played Rupert Mannion through the first three seasons: the man who made Rebecca want to burn the club down, and the best reason the show ever had to be angry. He died on 1 June 2026, aged 72, of complications of pneumonia; his daughters announced it. He had not filmed anything for Season 4, and nothing in the season was rewritten after he died. Brendan Hunt has since said they had an outside hope of bringing him back for the last episode and were told it would not be possible.
cards.why: So the pairing is not a design. An hour written long before his death, which happens to be the hour that takes away one of the pub’s fixtures, ends by marking the loss of the actor who played the show’s antagonist. The programme simply put the card where the episode had already arrived. If it lands hard, that is coincidence doing work no writer would have dared arrange.
cards.source: Anthony Head (1954–2026), Rupert Mannion in Seasons 1–3; the dedication closing Season 4, Episode 9.
cards.groundingNotes: Head’s death, age and cause, and the dedication card and its placement, are confirmed across five independent sources. The candidate’s suggestion that Season 4 had finished filming with him in it is corrected: he filmed nothing for the season and no storyline was altered after he died. Corrected again when Episode 10 was reviewed: this card previously said there had been no plan to bring him back, which Hunt’s own account contradicts — see s4e10-head-finale-plan. Season review 2026-10-12: Birth year corrected to 1954 (born 20 February 1954, per TheWrap and NBC LA). Hunt's words are an ‘outside hope’, not planned material.

cards.title: The song at Mae’s wake is Scottish, and older than the club
cards.moment: At the Crown & Anchor the Harrigan twins lead the room in ‘The Parting Glass’, and the pub joins in.
cards.idea: It is a Scottish song, not an Irish one. A distantly related tune, ‘Good Night, and God Be With Yow’, sits in a Scottish lute manuscript of roughly 1615 to 1635, and the first full text close to the modern words appears on a broadside dated 1654. It was the most popular parting song in Scotland until Burns wrote ‘Auld Lang Syne’ and took the job off it. The parting glass itself is the stirrup cup: the last drink handed up to a guest already on the horse, to get them home. The version the whole world sings now is heavily Irish and North American, which is how it can be sung for an English landlady in a London pub and still sound exactly right.
cards.why: Notice the small wrongness at the middle of it. This is a song for someone who is leaving — a drink pressed into the hand of a guest at the door — and it is being sung for someone who has already gone and cannot take it. Which is what a wake is. The hospitality carries on after the person it was for.
cards.source: ‘The Parting Glass’, traditional Scottish (Roud 3004); the Skene Manuscript, c. 1615–1635; a broadside of 1654. Sung at Mae’s wake in Season 4, Episode 10.
cards.groundingNotes: The performance at the wake is confirmed in five independent recaps. The song’s Scottish origin, the Skene Manuscript tune, the stirrup cup and its displacement by ‘Auld Lang Syne’ are corroborated beyond a single source; the 1654 date is given as approximate by some, so it is stated as a date on a broadside rather than the song’s birthday. Not claimed: that anyone in the scene remarks Mae was not Irish — only one recap reports it.

cards.title: The lie Ted tells his son is the lie Ted was told
cards.moment: Upstairs at the wake, Henry asks how Ted’s father died, and whether Ted might leave too. Ted says his dad fell down some stairs — which is the version Henry had already had from his Nana — and promises he is not going anywhere. He admits to Beard afterwards that he was not straight with him. After the match he goes back and tells Henry the truth.
cards.idea: Season 2’s ‘Man City’ is where the programme put the fact on the record: Ted, on the phone to Sharon after a heavy defeat, said his father died by suicide when Ted was sixteen. So the fall down the stairs is not Ted’s invention. It is his mother’s, repeated to her grandson, and Ted’s only contribution is to let it stand for an afternoon. Matt Lipsey directed both episodes.
cards.why: A family lie is rarely a decision. It is a thing somebody said once to protect a child, which then has to be said again every time that child's child asks. Ted is thirty years downstream of a sentence his mother chose, and the only way out of it is to be the one who stops repeating it. It takes him the length of a football match. (It is the same mother he told, in Season 3's ‘Mom City’, that her cheerfulness after his father's death had taught him to hide his own grief.)
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 10; and Season 2, Episode 8, ‘Man City’ (written by Jamie Lee, directed by Matt Lipsey), where Ted tells Sharon his father died by suicide when he was sixteen.
cards.groundingNotes: Confirmed in six independent write-ups, and the ‘Man City’ details from that episode’s own record. Two corrections to the research: no source makes Michelle the origin of the fall story — three name Ted’s mother, Henry’s Nana — and most report Ted repeating it rather than merely failing to correct it. Season review 2026-10-12: Cross-season link to s3e11-ted-grief-stepford-smiler added.

cards.tag: There is a book about this exact lie
cards.title: Philosophy has a name for what Ted does at the wake, and it does not let him off
cards.moment: The two halves of Ted’s answer to Henry: the fall down the stairs, upstairs at the pub, and the truth after the match.
