cards.idea: Sissela Bok’s Lying: Moral Choice in Public and Private Life (Pantheon, 1978; it won that year’s Orwell Award) is the standard philosophical treatment of the small protective lie, and it is where the modern philosophical use of ‘white lies’ comes from. Her position, as other philosophers summarise it, is that every lie carries a negative weight of its own. It can be outweighed — she does not say lying is never permitted — but it has to be outweighed rather than waved away, and her verdict is that most of the reasons people offer are not enough. The reason is trust: nobody has time to check everything they are told, so a lie spends something held in common.
cards.why: That is the exact shape of Ted's afternoon. A kind lie, told to a grieving boy, for reasons anybody would accept, and then withdrawn a few hours later, because the reasons turned out not to be good enough. Nobody argues him into it. He does the arithmetic Bok describes and comes out the other side of it on his own.
cards.source: Sissela Bok, Lying: Moral Choice in Public and Private Life (Pantheon, 1978). The episode makes no reference to Bok; she is this page’s lens, not the show’s.
cards.groundingNotes: Publication facts verified. Bok’s treatment of white lies, and the view that lies carry a negative weight which must be outweighed, are attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (citing Bok 1978) and a reference summary of the book. Deliberately left out: the claims often attached to her that liars overrate the benefit of their lies and underrate the damage to trust. Neither could be sourced to her text. Season review 2026-10-12: ‘Eleven-year-old’ removed: Henry's age is never given on screen (Deadline, ScreenRant and TVLine say 12).

cards.tag: A name for what all three of them are doing
cards.title: Psychology calls this generativity, and the hour runs three of it at once
cards.moment: Ted’s request to Rebecca, Alice’s promotion, and the Diamond Dogs sitting with Roy while he says out loud that he is frightened of being a bad father.
cards.idea: Erik Erikson built a model of a life in eight stages, each with its own conflict. The seventh, in middle adulthood, he called generativity against stagnation: the pull towards making or tending something that will outlast you — children, students, work handed on — set against the feeling of having stopped. The term is dated to 1950. This episode runs three versions of it and names none: Ted gives up the top job to be at his son’s matches, hands that job to the young coach he spent the season teaching, and Roy, given a toy soldier and a note, walks towards fatherhood rather than away from it.
cards.why: Erikson is this page’s lens, not the show’s reference — nothing in the episode mentions him. But a word for it helps, because from the inside the three stories look nothing like each other. One man is stepping back, one woman is stepping up, one man is terrified. Same motion. And the best line in the scene is Alice’s, and it is the smallest one: do not lie to your children, and do not bail when you feel useless.
cards.source: Erik Erikson’s seventh stage, generativity versus stagnation, in middle adulthood; the term dated to 1950. The episode makes no reference to Erikson.
cards.groundingNotes: The stage, its name, its opposing pole and its place in middle adulthood are corroborated by two sources; the 1950 date by one. Deliberately dropped: the book. The term is usually credited to Childhood and Society, but nothing consulted confirms that is where Erikson introduced it, so no book is named. Age boundaries differ between sources and are left out.

cards.tag: Two per cent, left in a will
cards.title: The landlady decides who owns the football club
cards.moment: At the shareholders' meeting Zelda produces her holding, and Hugo Riddles turns on her: the Milk sisters' stake goes to Rebecca, which leaves the two women level at forty-nine per cent each. Then Elaine Pinter, of Pinter & Sons, the firm whose sponsorship Rebecca saved in Episode 3, reads Mae's will. Mae leaves the Crown & Anchor to Baz, Jeremy and Paul, with a blunt instruction not to ruin it. And she leaves her shares in the club, two per cent, to Rebecca. That makes fifty-one.
cards.idea: Look at whose vote it turned out to be. Last week's episode spent its running time on the fact that Mae wanted to play football as a girl and was not allowed to, and on her turning down a seat in the owner's box to stand in the supporters' end instead. She had been refusing offers for those shares all along. The woman the game shut out is the one who keeps it out of the wrong hands, and she does it after she is dead, on paper, through a solicitor. Brendan Hunt has said that was the question the writers set themselves: how can Mae save the team from the grave?
cards.why: This is the quietest possible way to make that point and the episode takes it. No speech, no flashback, nobody saying how much she loved this club. A document is read aloud in a boardroom and the arithmetic comes out right. (Do not do the sums too hard. Deadline's own recapper pointed out they do not quite square with the 51% Rebecca kept in Season 3.)
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 10, the shareholders’ meeting and the reading of Mae’s will; the figures reported identically across eight write-ups.
cards.groundingNotes: Eight independent write-ups give the same arithmetic — Riddles turning, the 49/49 deadlock, Mae’s two per cent making 51 — and the bequest of the pub to the three regulars. The instruction not to ruin it comes from one source and is reported as such. Season review 2026-10-12: CORRECTED: Mae's shareholding was known before the will; she had refused to sell (Cosmopolitan via Yahoo, Fangirlish). Elaine Pinter of Pinter & Sons as executor per the transcript and a search-result summary of the MEAWW finale explainer. ‘Don't ruin it’ now two-sourced (the transcript, A.V. Club). Hunt's ‘from the grave’ question per Variety. The arithmetic caveat per Deadline's recap.

cards.title: The title is quoting Rebecca
cards.moment: Talking to Ted about Mae, Rebecca works her way round to it: they laugh, they hurt, they fall over, they get up, they are a mess — and being messy, she says, just means being alive. Everyone could do with being a bit more of it. Then she goes into her own office and asks Matthijs to marry her.
cards.idea: Brendan Hunt has confirmed this is the line the retitled episode is echoing. He calls it a nice little echo, and it is the reason the title is not simply a shrug about a landlady departing. Which makes this the hour’s stated argument rather than a good line in passing. Read the rest of the episode against it: a hundred-year-old pub handed to three men who drink in it, a football club decided by two per cent in a will, a father who lied to his son at a funeral, a manager who asks to be demoted.
cards.why: She says it and then does it, in the same scene, without stopping to check whether it is a good idea. That is the entire difference between having a philosophy and having one. Watch how little time passes between the speech and the proposal — and that it is she who asks.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 10, ‘Being Alive’; Rebecca’s line reported in three independent write-ups and named by Brendan Hunt as the echo behind the title.
cards.groundingNotes: The line is quoted in two independent write-ups and named by Hunt as what the title echoes; the proposal that follows is reported in three. Corrected from the research: Rebecca proposes to Matthijs, not the other way round.

cards.title: The most important conversation in the finale happens where you cannot hear it
cards.moment: After the match, Ted goes back to Henry and tells him the truth about his grandfather. The episode sets the scene up, lets Ted begin, and cuts away.
cards.idea: Four reviews flag it and three of them object; it is among the finale's most criticised choices, and one of many complaints behind the A.V. Club's C−, though IndieWire largely defends it. The complaint is fair. The programme spent four seasons arriving at a man able to say the thing out loud, and then does not let you hear him say it. The hour does something similar with the football: no recap reports a score for the final match, and Hunt has said the win that day was the sellout and that the game would not matter by then.
cards.why: Whether you forgive it depends on what you think the scene was for. Shown, it is a performance of honesty with an audience in the room. Withheld, it belongs to the two of them, and all you are given is that it happened — which is all Henry’s own children will ever have of it either. The show has form: it would rather hand you the consequence than the moment.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 10; the cut-away noted in four independent reviews, including the A.V. Club’s C− notice. Brendan Hunt on what the win was that day.
cards.groundingNotes: The cut-away and the A.V. Club grade are confirmed across four independent reviews. The match is held carefully and no result is asserted: eight write-ups give none and one says it is never revealed, while a single outlet states the women won. Season review 2026-10-12: Softened: the A.V. Club spreads its complaints widely; this is one of them. IndieWire's defence added.

cards.title: Ted asks to be demoted, not promoted
cards.moment: Ted turns up in Rebecca's office with biscuits and raises the newly open manager's job. Alice gets it. Ted and a freshly shaved Beard are her assistants, and Ted tells his son he is making changes so that he misses fewer of his games.
cards.idea: Several recaps read that line as Ted angling for the men's job Roy has just vacated. Hunt has corrected it twice: the position Ted was talking about was the women's, and it was open because he was leaving it. He added that sending Ted straight back to the men would have been a disservice to the sport, and, less comfortingly, that assistant coaches do not set their own schedules, so the time Ted thinks he is buying may not arrive. And look at the last shot of the nameplates: Alice, manager; Ted and Beard, assistant managers. The season opened on a grocery-store name tag that said assistant manager. Hunt says that bookend was Sudeikis's idea from the very start.
cards.why: A man who came to England to run things asks, at the end of the season, to stop running them. Remember the plaques he found in his father's house in Episode 1, the ones that told him his dad loved his work? Hunt says it is his father's plaque that turns him here, a reminder that you can be a little too devoted to your work. Same object, read the other way round, ten episodes later. Two small debts get settled too: the going-away present Ted had made for Alice back in Episode 2 and never handed over, and the business of his badly adjusted chair, which turns out to have been her all season. Hunt calls it Chekhov's chair.
cards.source: Season 4, Episode 10; Brendan Hunt correcting the men’s-team reading in two separate interviews.
cards.groundingNotes: The step down and Alice’s promotion are confirmed in seven independent write-ups, and Hunt corrects the men’s-job misreading in two separate interviews. Not asserted: what is inside the Episode 2 present — one recap says a plaque naming her manager, another a whistle. Season review 2026-10-12: CORRECTED: the hour does not open on the name tag; the season does, and the hour closes on the nameplates outside the coaches' office (ComicBasics; Deadline recap; Hunt to TheWrap and Variety on the bookend). The father's plaque per Hunt (Variety) and TVLine's recap; the award's name differs between them and is not given. The Episode 2 present is a nameplate per Hunt (TVLine) but a whistle per Deadline, so its contents stay unnamed. ‘Chekhov's chair’ per Hunt in two interviews. ‘Eleven-year-old’ removed: Henry's age is not given on screen.

cards.tag: It came from a son in the first place
cards.title: The toy Ted leaves Roy was a present from Henry
cards.moment: Clearing out his office, Roy finds a note from Ted saying he will be a good dad, and with it one of the little green army men. He puts it in his pocket and goes.
cards.idea: The army men arrive in Season 1’s second episode, ‘Biscuits’, in a care package from Henry: a bag of plastic soldiers sent to keep his father safe in a country Henry had never seen. Ted has been giving them away ever since. Rebecca got the first, stood on her desk between her and the door after a reporter ambushed her about Rupert. Sam got the second, for his birthday. There have been others along the way — one for Jamie, one left at the bottom of Sharon’s drink, one on the table the day Ted signed his divorce papers.
cards.why: So the object a frightened boy posted to his father, so that his father would be guarded, ends up in the pocket of a man who has just spent the episode asking a room full of men whether he will be any good at this. It travels the right way round. And nobody in the scene says a word of that; Roy simply reads a note, takes the soldier and leaves.
cards.source: Season 1, Episode 2, ‘Biscuits’, where Henry’s care package arrives; the note and the army man in Roy’s desk in Season 4, Episode 10.
cards.groundingNotes: The note and the army man are confirmed in four independent recaps; a fifth describes the object as a ‘little green statue’ and mentions no note, and is treated as the outlier. The origin in ‘Biscuits’ — a care package from Ted’s son, Rebecca first, Sam second — is confirmed by three sources, which also settles the research’s open question: no source places the bag in the pilot.

cards.tag: Her answer to death is attention
cards.title: The poem in Mae’s voice at the end is arguing with death
cards.moment: The closing montage, checking in on everybody, narrated by Annette Badland — Mae reading Mary Oliver’s ‘When Death Comes’.
cards.idea: The poem is in New and Selected Poems, the 1992 book that won Oliver the National Book Award. Its argument, paraphrased: death is coming, there is no negotiating with that, so the only question still open is what sort of life it finds when it arrives. Her answer is not courage, and it is not faith. It is attention. She wants to be able to say she went at the world astonished by it — married, as she puts it, to amazement — and the poem ends by refusing the other possibility, of having merely visited.
cards.why: That is this programme’s own creed in better words, and it is given to the character who got the least life out of it. Mae spent four seasons behind a bar watching other people do things. Handing her the poem about not having only visited is either very cruel or very generous, and the episode does not tell you which.
cards.source: Mary Oliver, ‘When Death Comes’, in New and Selected Poems (1992; National Book Award). Paraphrased here — the poem is in copyright.
cards.groundingNotes: Four recaps and a fifth naming Badland’s voice confirm the poem and the montage; the collection, year and award are confirmed from three sources. Not stated: a first magazine publication. One guide places it in the Virginia Quarterly Review in 1991, another gives 1992 in the collection, and the two could not be reconciled.

cards.title: The finale was renamed late, and the old name is still out there
cards.moment: The name on the episode you just watched, and the name Apple’s own press notes were still using while you watched it.
cards.idea: For most of production this hour was called ‘The Departing Lass’. Jason Sudeikis changed it to ‘Being Alive’ about a month before transmission. Brendan Hunt says the decision was Sudeikis’s entirely and that he was not walked through the reasoning, and that the change simply did not reach whoever puts the titles up. It didn’t: Apple’s viewing page says ‘Being Alive’ while its press episode guide still said ‘The Departing Lass’, and at least one recap published on the night of broadcast is filed under the old name.
cards.why: Worth knowing because the two titles point in opposite directions. ‘The Departing Lass’ is about Mae leaving. ‘Being Alive’ is about everybody who is still here, which is what the hour actually does with her death. Late retitles are usually an accident of scheduling. This one reads like somebody deciding, at the last minute, what the episode had turned out to be about.
cards.source: Apple TV’s episode listing and press guide; Brendan Hunt interviewed about the finale; a recap published under the earlier title.
cards.groundingNotes: The retitling is confirmed from four sources: Apple’s viewing page, its press guide, Hunt’s own account (about a month, Sudeikis’s call) and a recap filed under the old name. Deliberately not claimed: that the title card inside the episode still reads the old name. No source says what the card shows, and the lag Hunt describes is traceable to Apple’s listings.

cards.title: ‘Being Alive’ is also the last song in a musical about this exact problem
cards.moment: The episode’s title.
cards.idea: ‘Being Alive’ closes Stephen Sondheim’s Company (1970, book by George Furth). Robert is thirty-five and single and has spent the whole evening watching his married friends from a safe distance. In the song he stops watching. He asks to be needed, crowded, interrupted, hurt — asks for the mess rather than the quiet. Sondheim only got there on the fourth try: three earlier closing numbers were written and dropped, the last of them judged too bleak to end a show on.
cards.why: Nobody involved with the programme has said it meant Sondheim. Asked about the title, Brendan Hunt pointed at Rebecca's line in the episode, not at a musical. But the song exists and it is making the same argument: that the alternative to being hurt is not being alive. Three people in this hour choose the crowded version. Ted tells his son something that will hurt, Roy walks towards fatherhood, and Rebecca asks a man to marry her in her own office about ninety seconds after deciding to.
cards.source: Stephen Sondheim, ‘Being Alive’, from Company (1970). The connection to the show is unestablished.
cards.groundingNotes: The song is verified from two independent sources: Sondheim’s Company, 1970, book by George Furth, the closing number, reached on the fourth attempt. That the show intends the reference is NOT verified — Hunt credits Sudeikis and points at Rebecca’s dialogue, and Sondheim appears in none of the finale interviews. Presented as a resonance, never as an attribution. Season review 2026-10-12: Softened: one commentary piece (Mac Observer) now links the title to Sondheim, so the card says nobody involved with the show has, rather than that no source has.

cards.tag: Listen to the titles this week
cards.title: A different voice sings the theme over this one
cards.moment: The opening credits.
cards.idea: Brandi Carlile sings the theme instead of Marcus Mumford, who wrote it with the show’s composer Tom Howe and has sung it over the titles since 2020. Hunt’s reason is tonal: coming out of Mae’s wake and straight into the up-tempo original would have been, in his words, a bit abrupt, so the first cut of the episode used Jeff Tweedy’s spare acoustic version instead — the one from Season 2’s ‘Beard After Hours’, where the theme was also swapped out. It is the first time a woman has sung it. Carlile is a friend of Sudeikis’s and had worked on the show before, recording ‘Home’ from The Wiz for Season 3. Whether the change sticks is undecided; Hunt, calling this version a bit funereal, said they would have to see.
cards.why: A title sequence is the one part of a programme nobody is supposed to notice, which makes it a good place to put information. The season has spent ten episodes moving the show from the men’s team to the women’s. This is the first time that move reaches the ninety seconds that are identical every week.
cards.source: Brendan Hunt on the finale’s theme; the swap also noted in two independent reviews. Theme by Marcus Mumford and Tom Howe.
cards.groundingNotes: The swap is confirmed by Hunt and two independent reviews; the Tweedy substitution in ‘Beard After Hours’ is corroborated by that episode’s own record; Carlile’s earlier ‘Home’ cover is verified separately. Two research claims dropped: that Sudeikis specifically wanted a woman to sing it (the source says only that this is the first time one has), and a count of previous substitutions.

cards.tag: The scene that did not happen
cards.title: Rupert was meant to be in the room where the club changes hands
cards.moment: The shareholders’ meeting — the one part of the finale with a Rupert-shaped hole in it.
cards.idea: Brendan Hunt, who co-wrote the hour with Sudeikis, has said they had an outside hope of bringing Anthony Head back for the last episode, and that they were told it would not be possible. Head died on 1 June 2026, aged 72, of complications of pneumonia, after Season 4 had finished shooting; his daughters announced it four days later. Annette Badland said she had assumed he would be in the final season and had not known he was ill.
cards.why: Worth knowing because the boardroom scene plays slightly strangely without him. Rebecca's whole ownership of this club began as something taken off Rupert, and the hour that settles it for good has to do so with him absent and somebody else cast as the opponent. Hunt has not said where Rupert would have gone in the episode; this room is simply the obvious place.
cards.source: Brendan Hunt on the finale, in two separate interviews; Anthony Head (1954–2026), Rupert Mannion.
cards.groundingNotes: Hunt’s account — material written for Head in Episode 10, and being told he could not take part — is carried by two independent interviews, one of which also explains the Episode 9 placement of the tribute. Head’s death date, age and cause are confirmed separately. This supersedes Episode 9’s note that there had been no plan to bring him back. Season review 2026-10-12: CORRECTED: Hunt spoke of an outside hope, not planned material; the boardroom as Rupert's likely scene was an outlet's guess and is now labelled as this card's inference. The claim that Hunt explained the Episode 9 placement of the tribute is unsupported and removed. Birth year corrected to 1954.

cards.tag: The cameos are doing a job
cards.title: The men turning up to watch is the handover, and it was built that way
cards.moment: Nate in Ted’s office, the Diamond Dogs reconvening around Roy, and familiar faces in the stand at Nelson Road.
cards.idea: Hunt has said the men's appearances were meant as a passing-of-the-torch moment, the men supporting the women, and that it was held back for the finale on purpose, as the transition between what the show was and what it is now. He thinks it worked. Nate and Sam are the only returning players with lines; Sam's were a late addition, there to help Roy think about the Chelsea offer. Phil Dunster's Jamie is absent for what Hunt calls a logic thing: Jamie lives in Spain and plays for Barcelona, and had already turned up in Episode 6.
cards.why: Easy to file as fan service, and the episode gives you every excuse — Nate is married with a daughter and coaching Poland, Dani and Sam and Isaac are in the crowd, Alice joins the Diamond Dogs as a cat. But watch where they are all standing. Not on the pitch. In the stands, at somebody else’s match, applauding. That is what handing a thing over looks like when it is done properly.
cards.source: Brendan Hunt on the finale’s cameos, in two separate interviews; the appearances reported across five independent recaps.
